The Aerosense measurement system uses low-cost, low-power MEMS sensors to measure local pressures, blade motions, and inflow conditions on wind turbine blades.
The system is composed of sensor nodes installed on the blades, a base station that collects and transmits the data, and a digital twin system for data processing and analysis.
The sensor nodes include 40 absolute pressure sensors, 5 differential pressure sensors, and a 9-axis inertial measurement unit.
Careful calibration of the absolute pressure sensors can achieve an accuracy of 1% of the full-scale pressure range.
Corrections are required to account for atmospheric pressure variations, hydrostatic pressure changes due to blade rotation, and potential influence of centrifugal acceleration.
The measurements on the 7kW wind turbine showed significant variations in the pressure distribution during a single blade rotation, even under stable wind conditions.
The Aerosense system uses a hybrid method based on inviscid flow theory to infer the local angle of attack and wind speed without requiring a reference pressure measurement.
Photogrammetry is used to precisely measure the 3D shape of the blade section and the positions of the pressure sensors.
The Aerosense system is designed to be easy to install, non-intrusive, and cost-effective compared to previous field measurement systems for wind turbine blades.
The atmospheric pressure is about 50 times higher than the dynamic pressure on a 5MW wind turbine, while the hydrostatic pressure variation is about 40% of the dynamic pressure.
The pressure drift of the barometers is about 5% of the dynamic pressure on a 5MW wind turbine.
The Aerosense system can measure pressure fluctuations at up to 500 points during one rotation of a larger multi-megawatt wind turbine blade.
The differential pressure sensors in the Aerosense system have a sampling rate of 1.2 kHz to capture the dynamics of the turbulent inflow conditions.
The Aerosense system is designed to monitor not only the aerodynamic performance but also the structural health of the wind turbine blades.
Previous field measurement campaigns on wind turbine blades have been limited by the complexity and cost of embedding sensors and wiring inside the blades.
